scenes.text: In seahorses, it's the dad who gets pregnant and gives birth.
After an elaborate courtship dance, the female places her eggs into a pouch near the base of his tail.
Inside this brood pouch, the father keeps the growing babies safe.
He supplies them with oxygen and nutrients while they develop.
The pouch even forms a placenta-like tissue, a bit like a mammal's womb.
A study found that this tissue grows from the father's skin.
He also slowly changes the fluid in the pouch until it's like seawater, so the babies are ready for the ocean.
Depending on the species, pregnancy lasts from about ten days to six weeks.
When it's time, he bends and jerks his whole body, flushing water through the pouch.
Many hundreds of tiny babies can shoot out in a short time.
They look like miniature adults and get no more care from their parents.
Only a tiny fraction of them survive to adulthood.
And soon after giving birth, the dad can be pregnant all over again.
Their close cousins, the pipefish, also have dads that carry the young.
Should more animal dads do the heavy lifting? Tell me below.

title: In seahorses, the dads give birth 🐠
caption: Female seahorses put their eggs in the male's pouch, where he supplies oxygen and nutrients. Then he gives birth to hundreds of babies and can get pregnant again soon after.
